Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says he used Claude to prove the Riemann hypothesis, math's most famous open problem for 167 years, with a proof formalized in Lean that spans over 250,000 pages. Just hours later, Stanford researchers published an independent, entirely human competing proof, and mathematicians are now checking whether either one holds up.

en.title: AI memory is helping me — and also seems to trap me
en.summary: AI memory brings convenience, but it also carries a hidden risk of trapping people. After the author added a "novice lecturer" tag, the AI kept limiting opportunities to the training track, reinforcing the stereotype and even leading the author to gradually identify with this single identity. This reflection is a warning for heavy Agent users: in human-AI coexistence, don't let AI's memory box in your broader potential.

en.title: The comparison table already answers half of it: Neon scores 61 on the Artificial Analysis quality index, slightly above Carbon's 60, and its input price is a dollar cheaper ($3 vs. $4), making Neon the better value for everyday coding and agent tasks. But Carbon is still positioned for "the hardest long-horizon projects and deep research," which suggests it isn't being fully replaced by Neon — the two are divided by role.
en.summary: The comparison table already answers half the question: Neon scores 61 on the Artificial Analysis quality index, slightly above Carbon’s 60, and its input price is a dollar cheaper ($3 vs. $4), making Neon the better value for everyday coding and agent tasks. But Carbon is still positioned for “the hardest long-horizon projects and deep research,” which suggests it isn’t being fully replaced by Neon but rather that the two are split by role. Argon’s removal is probably not an oversight—some commenters note that Carbon was built with RL on top of Argon, and Argon is reportedly also set to be retired from Antigravity in December. Google’s problem now isn’t that its models aren’t strong enough; it’s that the three-tier naming makes it impossible to tell which model should do what.
en.reason: Neon's Artificial Analysis quality index of 61 edges Carbon's 60 while its $3 input price undercuts Carbon's $4, making Neon the better value for daily coding and agent tasks, though Carbon still targets the hardest long-horizon projects and deep research.

en.summary:
These terms keep popping up lately—here's a plain-English explainer:

LLM
Large language model. ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, DeepSeek—the AI that can chat and write—all fall under LLM.

Agent
AI that can break a task into parts and execute it in multiple steps. It's not just answer-one-question-at-a-time; it can plan on its own, call tools, and get something done.

Coding Agent
An Agent built specifically to write code, fix code, and run projects. Examples include Claude Code and Cursor. This is a different track from a Personal Agent.

Personal Agent
An Agent that manages your email, calendar, and information—a personal assistant. A separate path from Coding Agents.

Tool Use
The ability of AI to actively call external tools—for example, searching on its own or executing code…
en.reason: A plain-language glossary explains five AI terms, noting that ChatGPT, Claude, Grok and DeepSeek are all LLMs, that Claude Code and Cursor are Coding Agents, and that Personal Agents managing email and calendars follow a separate path from Coding Agents.

Then I went back and checked the original Contra leaderboard, and #1 is still the anonymous Gestalt. The Riemann Hypothesis writeup only mentions Claude, too — no idea which version.

en.title: How RSI lets AI improve itself
en.summary:
How Does RSI Let AI Improve Itself?

I've been building DocFlow, a full-stack hands-on project that combines Agent, RAG, and knowledge graphs. It's been tested to support real-time collaboration for hundreds of users and can import Word (DOCX) and PDF files. The Agent can retrieve materials, rewrite documents, and operate tables. Under the hood, a main Agent coordinates while sub-agents verify in parallel and review results, alongside automatic context compression, long- and short-term memory, and task recovery. The RAG side covers parent-child chunking, BM25 + vector hybrid retrieval, RRF fusion, reranking, and source citation tracing. It's suited to anyone who wants to dig into the source code and build AI applications hands-on.

I've also put together 80 articles on Agent development, 72 on RAG, and 70 on knowledge graphs — 222 learning materials in total, spanning fundamentals to engineering practice. You can learn by doing alongside the source code. If you're interested, add me on WeChat at yunmz777 to learn about the project and accompanying materials, and let's talk AI development.

We give AI a task, it spots an error and keeps revising until the result meets the requirements — this process is already commonplace. But once the task ends, does that correction change the system, and can the next round of improvement...
en.reason: RSI lets an AI keep a change only after it is verified, illustrated by a Coding Agent that edits its own editing tool, adds a locate check plus before-and-after validation, and distinguishes task capability from improvement capability.

en.title: Hand-Building an Agent (Part 4): Learning to Remember — What to Do When the Context Is Full, and How to Recall the Last Round
en.summary:
Building an Agent by Hand (Part 4): A Little Memory — What to Do When the Context Fills Up, and How to Remember the Last Time

> Part 4 of the 10-part Building an Agent by Hand series. [Series intro and table of contents](https://juejin.cn/post/7708787125920006194 "https://juejin.cn/post/7708787125920006194") | Previous: [Open Your Eyes — Context Is the Entire World It Sees](https://juejin.cn/post/7709075612398125066 "https://juejin.cn/post/7709075612398125066")
Figure 4-1: the series map. This installment is still inside the blue box: eyes.
The previous post left two open questions: the trajectory only grows and never shrinks, so eventually it won't fit; and once the program closes, it remembers nothing.
These two problems are really about the same thing: memory. I used to assume "memory" was a feature of the model — flip a switch and it remembers. Only after getting this far did I understand that the model has no such feature. As the first post explained, its parameters are fixed once training ends, and every request is brand new to it. What we call memory is entirely a matter of working on the context.
*
en.reason: A 600-character context budget forces a choice among trimming, compression and external storage, with compaction demoed by splitting at the last user message and a memory file letting v0.4 recall the previous session.

en.summary: The comparison table already answers half the question: Neon scores 61 on the Artificial Analysis quality index, slightly above Carbon’s 60, and its input price is a dollar cheaper ($3 vs. $4), making Neon the better value for everyday coding and agent tasks. But Carbon is still positioned for “the hardest long-horizon projects and deep research,” which suggests it isn’t being fully replaced by Neon but rather that the two are split by role. Argon’s removal is probably not an oversight—some commenters note that Carbon was built with RL on top of Argon, and Argon is reportedly also set to be retired from Antigravity in December. Google’s problem now isn’t that its models aren’t strong enough; it’s that the three-tier naming makes it impossible to tell which model should do what.
en.reason: Neon's Artificial Analysis quality index of 61 edges Carbon's 60 while its $3 input price undercuts Carbon's $4, making Neon the better value for daily coding and agent tasks, though Carbon still targets the hardest long-horizon projects and deep research.

en.summary:
These terms keep popping up lately—here's a plain-English explainer:

LLM
Large language model. ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, DeepSeek—the AI that can chat and write—all fall under LLM.

Agent
AI that can break a task into parts and execute it in multiple steps. It's not just answer-one-question-at-a-time; it can plan on its own, call tools, and get something done.

Coding Agent
An Agent built specifically to write code, fix code, and run projects. Examples include Claude Code and Cursor. This is a different track from a Personal Agent.

Personal Agent
An Agent that manages your email, calendar, and information—a personal assistant. A separate path from Coding Agents.

Tool Use
The ability of AI to actively call external tools—for example, searching on its own or executing code…
en.reason: A plain-language glossary explains five AI terms, noting that ChatGPT, Claude, Grok and DeepSeek are all LLMs, that Claude Code and Cursor are Coding Agents, and that Personal Agents managing email and calendars follow a separate path from Coding Agents.

en.summary:
The AI topics most worth prioritizing in 2026 fall into three main areas: AI Agents, post-training for LLM reasoning, and multimodal plus practical engineering implementation (RAG, tool calling, evaluation, etc.). These offer more long-term value than simply learning one more, larger model.

1. Getting started (no prior experience / non-technical background)
• Elements of AI (University of Helsinki + MinnaLearn)
Completely free, with no math or programming required. It covers what AI can and cannot do, the basic principles, and societal impact. You can earn a free certificate after completing it (the Introduction section).

en.title: Saw a Saga 6 benchmark chart — holy crap, Fable 5.2 has been out for how long, and its own sibling model already beats it by 580 points?
en.summary:
Saw the Saga 6 benchmark chart and holy crap — Fable 5.2 has barely been out, and it's already been beaten by its own company's model by 580 points??

Then I went back and checked the original Contra leaderboard, and #1 is still the anonymous Gestalt. The Riemann Hypothesis writeup only mentions Claude, too — no idea which version.

Everyone take this as gossip for now. But if it really is the same internal model, can Anthropic sit out a round and let someone else win for once 😂 https://t.co/HtMm4WFrfW
en.reason: A Saga 6 benchmark chart claims Fable 5.2 trails a sibling model by 580 points, while the Contra leaderboard still has anonymous Gestalt first and the Riemann Hypothesis note names only Claude, version unspecified.

en.title: How RSI lets AI improve itself
en.summary:
How Does RSI Let AI Improve Itself?

I've been building DocFlow, a full-stack hands-on project that combines Agent, RAG, and knowledge graphs. It's been tested to support real-time collaboration for hundreds of users and can import Word (DOCX) and PDF files. The Agent can retrieve materials, rewrite documents, and operate tables. Under the hood, a main Agent coordinates while sub-agents verify in parallel and review results, alongside automatic context compression, long- and short-term memory, and task recovery. The RAG side covers parent-child chunking, BM25 + vector hybrid retrieval, RRF fusion, reranking, and source citation tracing. It's suited to anyone who wants to dig into the source code and build AI applications hands-on.

I've also put together 80 articles on Agent development, 72 on RAG, and 70 on knowledge graphs — 222 learning materials in total, spanning fundamentals to engineering practice. You can learn by doing alongside the source code. If you're interested, add me on WeChat at yunmz777 to learn about the project and accompanying materials, and let's talk AI development.

We give AI a task, it spots an error and keeps revising until the result meets the requirements — this process is already commonplace. But once the task ends, does that correction change the system, and can the next round of improvement...
en.reason: RSI lets an AI keep a change only after it is verified, illustrated by a Coding Agent that edits its own editing tool, adds a locate check plus before-and-after validation, and distinguishes task capability from improvement capability.

Published Time: 2026-11-19T05:56:13+00:00
> 《手搓 Agent》系列第 4 篇，共 10 篇。[系列导读与目录](https://juejin.cn/post/7708787125920006194 "https://juejin.cn/post/7708787125920006194")｜上一篇：[睁开眼睛——上下文是它看到的全部世界](https://juejin.cn/post/7709075612398125066 "https://juejin.cn/post/7709075612398125066")
图 4-1 系列地图。这一篇还在蓝色的框里：眼睛。
上一篇留下两个问题：轨迹只增不减，早晚装不下；程序一关，它什么都不记得。
这两个问题说的其实是同一件事：记性。我原来以为“记忆”是模型的一项功能，打开某个开关它就记住了。学到这里才明白，模型没有这项功能。第一篇讲过，它的参数训练完就固定了，每次请求对它都是全新的。所谓记性，全是在上下文上做文章。
*

en.title: Hand-Building an Agent (Part 4): Learning to Remember — What to Do When the Context Is Full, and How to Recall the Last Round
en.summary:
Building an Agent by Hand (Part 4): A Little Memory — What to Do When the Context Fills Up, and How to Remember the Last Time

> Part 4 of the 10-part Building an Agent by Hand series. [Series intro and table of contents](https://juejin.cn/post/7708787125920006194 "https://juejin.cn/post/7708787125920006194") | Previous: [Open Your Eyes — Context Is the Entire World It Sees](https://juejin.cn/post/7709075612398125066 "https://juejin.cn/post/7709075612398125066")
Figure 4-1: the series map. This installment is still inside the blue box: eyes.
The previous post left two open questions: the trajectory only grows and never shrinks, so eventually it won't fit; and once the program closes, it remembers nothing.
These two problems are really about the same thing: memory. I used to assume "memory" was a feature of the model — flip a switch and it remembers. Only after getting this far did I understand that the model has no such feature. As the first post explained, its parameters are fixed once training ends, and every request is brand new to it. What we call memory is entirely a matter of working on the context.
*
en.reason: A 600-character context budget forces a choice among trimming, compression and external storage, with compaction demoed by splitting at the last user message and a memory file letting v0.4 recall the previous session.
